title: Windows Firewall Rule Changes
exclusions: Reports locally added, modified, and deleted Windows Defender Firewall rules only when Windows writes Security events 4946, 4947, and 4948 under `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change`. Microsoft states that these three events do not generate for individual rule changes delivered through Group Policy. The use case therefore does not prove the effective firewall policy, rule precedence, whether a rule is enabled, direction, action, protocol, port, address, application, service, interface, edge-traversal setting, or who performed the change; the documented event payload supplies profile, rule ID, and rule name but no Subject/actor block. It does not detect firewall-service stop, profile change, default-policy reset, setting change, ignored rule, failed rule application, Intune/MDM policy intent, non-Microsoft host firewalls, network firewalls, packet allow/drop activity, or changes that occurred while auditing or collection was unavailable. Operational-channel events such as 2004/2005/2006 are not interchangeable with the primary Security audit contract and 2033 is not treated as a firewall-disabled event. A result proves only that Splunk received a matching audit event; it does not prove authorization, malicious intent, current rule state, continuous endpoint coverage, or regulatory compliance. The catalogue SPL contains no exception lookup.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_firewall_local_rule_changes_4946_4948` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch and triggered-alert history; each result row with endpoint, action, rule ID, rule name, changed profile, EventCode, event-record ID, source, and event time; and a protected drilldown or immutable export of the matching raw Security event. Also retain effective Advanced Audit Policy/GPO evidence, endpoint inventory and source-health results, the effective `[WinEventLog://Security]` input and add-on versions/configuration, the corresponding `Get-NetFirewallRule` or `wf.msc` observation, approved change or incident disposition, bounded notification exceptions, and dated positive/negative control output. For deletions, preserve pre-change inventory or change records because the current firewall store may no longer contain the rule. These artifacts demonstrate the documented event-processing path for records received by Splunk. This documentation-only review created no Windows event, Splunk search result, alert, firewall state, or production evidence and does not establish complete collection or authorization.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index and fixed UTC interval, replay three sanitized XML-rendered Security events from one endpoint: 4946 with `RuleId={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`, `RuleName=UC-1.2.28 Local Allow Test`, and `ProfileChanged=Private`; 4947 with the same rule ID/name and `ProfileChanged=Private`; and 4948 with the same rule ID/name and profile. Give them distinct `EventRecordID` values. Run a copy of the primary SPL with only the index changed. Expect exactly three rows ordered newest first, actions `added`, `modified`, and `deleted`, the same non-null rule identity and endpoint, and the corresponding event-record IDs. Confirm no actor field is invented.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate isolated interval, replay Security events 4950 (firewall setting changed), 4954 (Group Policy settings applied), and 4949 (defaults restored); Operational-channel events 2004, 2005, 2006, and 2033; a System-channel event whose EventCode is 4946; and an otherwise matching Security 4946 with blank `RuleId`. The primary search must return zero rows. Then replay a valid 4946 for an approved administration test and confirm the base search still returns it; any exact, time-bounded change-ticket exception may alter only downstream notification and must not erase the event or base result.

dataSources: Primary source: Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing events 4946 (local firewall rule added), 4947 (local rule modified), and 4948 (local rule deleted) from each in-scope endpoint's Security channel after Success auditing is enabled for `Policy Change > Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change`. Collect locally with a Splunk Universal Forwarder `[WinEventLog://Security]` input and normalize with the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) into the deployment-local `index=wineventlog`. The primary XML contract is `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`; required event fields are `EventCode`, `ProfileChanged`, `RuleId`, `RuleName`, `Computer` or `host`, and `EventRecordID` or `RecordNumber`. Windows event collection is checkpointed and event-driven, not an API, HEC, scripted, or modular-input poll.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), release 8.1.2 or a later platform-compatible release whose XML Security-event extraction has been regression-tested locally. Deploy collection configuration to the Windows forwarders and the add-on's parsing/search-time knowledge to the tiers required by the topology. Splunkbase compatibility changes by add-on release; qualify the exact Windows, forwarder, add-on, and Splunk platform combination. No premium app is required.
spl:
index=wineventlog source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog EventCode IN (4946,4947,4948)
| eval action=case(EventCode=4946,"added",EventCode=4947,"modified",EventCode=4948,"deleted"), endpoint=coalesce(Computer,ComputerName,dest,host), rule_id=coalesce(RuleId,RuleID), rule_name=RuleName, profile_changed=ProfileChanged, event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber)
| where isnotnull(endpoint) AND len(trim(endpoint))>0 AND isnotnull(rule_id) AND len(trim(rule_id))>0
| table _time endpoint action rule_id rule_name profile_changed EventCode event_record_id source
| sort 0 - _time
description: Reports locally added, modified, and deleted Windows Defender Firewall rules from Security audit events 4946, 4947, and 4948. It preserves the endpoint, action, stable rule identifier, displayed rule name, affected profile, EventCode, and event-record identity without claiming unavailable actor, port, direction, application, or effective-policy details.
value: Unexpected local firewall changes can expose a service, weaken endpoint isolation, interrupt an application, or support defense evasion. A precise rule-identity report lets security and Windows teams reconcile each observed change with approved administration and pivot to the current rule definition, while honest payload limits prevent a sparse audit event from being presented as full configuration evidence.
implementation: Enable Success for `Policy Change > Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change` through controlled policy on every in-scope endpoint; collect the Security channel as XML with the Microsoft Windows add-on; verify 4946/4947/4948 field extraction and endpoint coverage; then save `windows_firewall_local_rule_changes_4946_4948` and run it every five minutes over a delayed ten-minute window. Review every result against change records and current firewall state; apply only exact, expiring exceptions in downstream notification.
visualization: Lead with endpoint collection and audit-policy health. Show a newest-first rule-change table with `_time`, endpoint, action, rule name, rule ID, changed profile, EventCode, and event-record ID; a 24-hour action timeline; and 30-day counts by endpoint, action, rule name, and profile. Drill down to the raw Security event, current `Get-NetFirewallRule -Name <rule_id>` or `wf.msc` state, and the change/incident disposition. Do not display actor, port, direction, or allow/block labels unless separately corroborated.
schema: Microsoft Windows Security events 4946, 4947, and 4948; raw event contract only
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the authoritative rule. No validated accelerated CIM dataset is claimed to preserve the exact Security source, local-only 4946/4947/4948 semantics, endpoint, profile, rule ID/name, and event-record identity. The previous generic `Change.All_Changes` count could return unrelated changes and did not enforce this contract. Keep the raw search authoritative; use a custom summary only after it retains every output field and passes event-level parity tests.

knownFalsePositives:
A correctly parsed 4946/4947/4948 row is not a false Windows event merely because the change is approved. False positives arise when downstream handling labels every local rule change malicious or pages on routine administration without context.

1. **Application installation, upgrade, repair, or removal** — MSI installers and vendor updaters can add, modify, or delete local rules needed by an application. Require the exact rule ID/name, endpoint scope, package/change record, installer identity from separate process telemetry, and approved interval. Do not permanently allow-list a vendor display name because names are mutable and reusable.

2. **Endpoint management, security, VPN, remote-support, or backup tooling** — An approved management agent can maintain local rules outside Group Policy. Verify the exact product deployment job, signed package, rule identity, target collection, and time. Suppress only that rule ID and bounded job window; unexpected endpoints or actions remain reviewable.

3. **Windows role or feature enablement** — Enabling Hyper-V, WSL, IIS, Remote Desktop, network discovery, or another Windows component can create or update rules. Correlate with the feature-change record and inspect the current rule. Do not infer the responsible component from the rule name alone.

4. **Administrator troubleshooting or emergency response** — Windows/network staff may create a temporary diagnostic rule or remove a dangerous rule during an incident. Require named authorization, endpoint, rule ID, intended settings, expiry, and restoration evidence. Preserve the event even when the action is justified.

5. **Golden-image build, provisioning, or test automation** — Image pipelines and disposable labs can intentionally generate repeated local-rule events. Use a separately named non-production scope or exact asset/build-job exception. Host-wide and subnet-wide production suppressions are unsafe.

6. **Duplicate collection or event replay** — Local forwarding plus WEF, checkpoint reset, or fixture replay can create duplicate Splunk rows. Compare originating computer, EventRecordID, rule ID, `_raw`, and `_indextime`; repair collection ownership instead of broad `dedup` that could hide distinct modifications.

7. **Rule churn with the same name** — An installer can delete and recreate a rule, producing multiple legitimate events with different IDs. Reconcile the full sequence and current store. A familiar name does not make a new rule ID trustworthy.

**Safe suppression:** keep `windows_firewall_local_rule_changes_4946_4948` unfiltered. Apply a version-controlled `windows_firewall_rule_change_exceptions.csv` only in downstream notification, keyed as narrowly as possible by endpoint, rule ID, action, owner, ticket, numeric `valid_from`, and `valid_until`. Reject wildcard endpoints, rule-name-only matches, open-ended dates, and actor-based exceptions because these events do not supply an actor. Log and periodically review every suppressed match.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Microsoft MPSSVC audit-policy and events 4946/4947/4948 documentation, Windows firewall tooling, Splunk Windows event-log collection and add-on documentation, and MITRE ATT&CK; no Windows firewall mutation, audit-policy deployment, fixture replay, Splunk SPL execution, alert delivery, CIM mapping, production validation, or Microsoft/Windows/Splunk/network-security SME runtime sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: The primary scheduled search filters an already collected Security channel to three low-volume EventCodes over a short delayed window. Endpoint-wide Security collection volume, retention, and any separate firewall-state inventory are larger shared costs; no CIM acceleration is claimed.
sources: raw-event saved search and protected drilldown

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and authoritative event contract

Assign Windows endpoint, firewall-policy, Splunk collection, detection-content, and response owners. Inventory every in-scope Windows client and server and identify whether local firewall rules are permitted, centrally managed, or prohibited. This use case is specifically the local-rule audit trail. Microsoft documents Security event 4946 for a locally added rule, 4947 for a modified rule, and 4948 for a deleted rule under **Policy Change > Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change**. Microsoft also states that these events do not generate when individual rules are added, modified, or deleted through Group Policy. If the control objective is effective policy or GPO drift, obtain a separate periodic firewall-state/GPO inventory; do not reinterpret missing 4946–4948 events as proof that no policy changed.

Enable Success auditing for `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change` through a reviewed GPO or local policy and confirm effective state on representative endpoints with `auditpol /get /subcategory:"MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change"`. Preserve `gpresult` or equivalent policy evidence. Size and retain the Security channel for the endpoint's broader audit policy, not just these low-volume events. Install a Splunk Universal Forwarder and a platform-compatible Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows. Release 8.1.2 documents the XML input behavior used here; test the exact Windows, forwarder, add-on, parsing-tier, search-tier, and Splunk platform combination. This editorial review did not run that stack, so no `splunkVersions` claim is made.

Give the collection service only the rights required to read the Security channel. Give the detection role read access to the target index and saved search. Restrict raw-event and exception-lookup access because endpoint names, policy details, and operational rule names can reveal security architecture. Responders do not need local-administrator or GPO-edit rights merely to view the report.

## Step 1 — Configure Security-channel collection and source health

Deploy a controlled local override rather than editing an add-on `default` file. A representative endpoint stanza is:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Security]
disabled = 0
start_from = oldest
current_only = 0
checkpointInterval = 5
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
```

Verify the winning configuration with `splunk btool inputs list WinEventLog://Security --debug`. XML rendering is the primary contract. Under the documented add-on behavior, channel identity is `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security` while the source type is `XmlWinEventLog`; the channel-specific source string is not the source type. Windows Event Log collection is event-driven and checkpointed. There is no 300-second API poll, HEC token, or scripted-input response to count.

After policy and input deployment, verify broad source health independently from firewall-rule changes:

```spl
index=wineventlog source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" earliest=-15m
| stats count min(_time) as first_event max(_time) as last_event values(sourcetype) as sourcetypes by host
```

An endpoint can have no local firewall changes for months, so zero 4946–4948 events is not a heartbeat. Reconcile forwarder/deployment inventory, broad Security-channel activity, queue status, and expected endpoint identity. If Windows Event Forwarding is used, preserve the originating `Computer` field and prove that events are not all attributed to the collector. Avoid simultaneous local and WEF collection unless duplicate ownership and event identity are explicitly handled.

Inspect representative 4946, 4947, and 4948 records with `| table _time host source sourcetype EventCode ProfileChanged RuleId RuleName Computer EventRecordID`. The documented payload provides profile, rule ID, and rule name. It does not provide the actor, executable path, direction, action, protocol, port, address, or enabled state. Do not fabricate those fields from host, rule name, or unrelated operational events. Use a separate state snapshot such as `Get-NetFirewallRule` plus associated filter cmdlets when the response workflow needs full rule semantics.

## Step 2 — Save, schedule, and understand the raw-event search

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_firewall_local_rule_changes_4946_4948`. Schedule it every five minutes over a delayed closed interval such as `earliest=-10m@m latest=-1m@m`, adjusted only after measuring forwarding latency. Trigger on any result. Preserve the raw-event drilldown and use endpoint plus event-record ID as the event identity; rule ID identifies the firewall rule, not an individual audit record.

Understanding this SPL: the base search accepts only the XML Security source, XML Windows source type, and three authoritative EventCodes. `case` translates 4946/4947/4948 to `added`/`modified`/`deleted`. `coalesce` tolerates documented field aliases for endpoint, rule ID, and event-record identity without assigning nonexistent semantics. The `where` clause enforces the minimum evidentiary contract: an endpoint and rule ID must exist. The table retains every field needed to locate the raw event. `sort 0` requests a complete newest-first ordering rather than the default sort cap.

There is no count threshold and no claim that one event is malicious. Route every base result to review or a lower-severity change-control workflow. A downstream high-priority analytic may enrich the rule ID using a separately collected current-state inventory and approved-rule baseline, but it must preserve the original sparse event and disclose when deleted rules cannot be queried. Do not label a rule inbound, allow, internet-exposed, or process-specific from these events alone.

No CIM search is supplied. A generic `Change.All_Changes` count cannot be assumed to preserve the exact 4946–4948 source, rule ID, profile, event-record identity, and local-versus-GPO scope. If a deployment creates a custom normalized dataset, validate event-level parity and field semantics before using it, but retain the raw search as the authoritative report. Do not enable data-model acceleration solely for this use case.

Keep the base search unsuppressed. Apply `windows_firewall_rule_change_exceptions.csv` only in downstream notification, with exact endpoint/rule ID/action and bounded activation/expiry. Preserve exception-match details and continue showing suppressed records in the audit dashboard. Alert throttling should use the saved-search result identity, not hide later modifications to the same rule.

## Step 3 — Validate events, boundaries, and current-state corroboration

Run the positive and negative `controlTest` scenarios in an isolated index and absolute time range. Assert exactly three positive rows, exact action translation, non-null rule IDs/endpoints, and distinct event-record IDs. Assert that 4949, 4950, 4954, operational-channel events, a wrong-channel event, and a malformed event produce no rows. Keep expected and actual output, raw fixtures, search revision, job ID, add-on version, and reviewer disposition.

For a live lab control, use a disposable endpoint under Windows/firewall-owner approval. Create a uniquely named local rule with `New-NetFirewallRule`, modify it with `Set-NetFirewallRule`, and delete it with `Remove-NetFirewallRule`. Use a non-disruptive program/port and do not expose a service to an untrusted network. Compare with the **Windows Defender Firewall interface** in `wf.msc` and with **Event Viewer > Windows Logs > Security**, then match the Splunk EventCode, UTC time, endpoint, profile, rule ID, rule name, and EventRecordID. Query `Get-NetFirewallRule -Name <rule-id>` for current state. The deleted rule may no longer be present, so retain the pre-delete state and command/change record.

Repeat with a GPO-delivered test rule in an isolated OU if GPO scope matters. Confirm that the per-rule 4946/4947/4948 expectation is not used for that path; use policy/application evidence such as 4954 and an effective-state inventory instead. Also test audit policy disabled, forwarder interruption/restart, checkpoint continuity, duplicate local/WEF routes, XML field extraction, endpoint identity, delayed arrival, and role-based raw access. A successful synthetic search does not prove endpoint fleet coverage.

Do not use production firewall changes solely to make an alert fire. Record Windows/add-on/forwarder/Splunk versions, effective audit/input configurations, test endpoint, exact commands or fixture hashes, UTC bounds, expected/actual rows, raw event IDs, current-state comparison, failures, and approver. Keep `status=draft` until runtime and SME acceptance is complete.

## Step 4 — Operationalize review, response, visualization, and evidence

Put endpoint source/audit health before the change table. Build the newest-first table and trends specified in `visualization`, with raw-event and current-state drilldowns. Avoid a “firewall disabled” tile: none of the three events has that meaning. Avoid an “unauthorized” count unless every row was actually reconciled to a policy/change source. Measure expected administrative volume before selecting page severity.

The runbook should: (1) verify the original Security event and endpoint identity; (2) confirm local versus GPO/MDM management; (3) retrieve the current rule and associated port/address/application filters when the rule still exists; (4) compare approved baseline, software deployment, endpoint-management, and change records; (5) correlate separate process creation, PowerShell, service, package, sign-in, EDR, and network telemetry to identify an actor or cause; (6) assess exposure and business impact; and (7) record authorized, benign-but-unexpected, collection artifact, or suspicious disposition. ATT&CK T1562.004 is an investigative hypothesis only when corroboration shows defense impairment; a routine 4946 does not prove adversary behavior.

Do not automatically delete, disable, recreate, or alter a rule; stop the firewall service; isolate the endpoint; or roll back GPO from this sparse event alone. A deleted rule may have been restrictive, and an added rule may have been protective. Windows/network/security owners must review full rule semantics and dependencies. Preserve the raw event and pre-remediation state before authorized containment.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` under local retention and access policy. The advisory 90-day cost value is not a legal mandate. Review collection, policy scope, saved search, exceptions, and dashboards after Windows builds, add-on upgrades, XML/classic rendering changes, WEF topology changes, firewall management migrations, or rule-governance changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot without weakening the contract

- **No Security events during an approved local-rule test:** verify the effective `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change` Success setting, inspect the endpoint Security log first, confirm the rule was local rather than GPO-managed, then check the WinEventLog stanza, checkpoint, forwarding route, index, and time bounds.
- **Security events exist but the SPL returns none:** inspect exact `source`, `sourcetype`, EventCode, and case-sensitive extracted field names. If Classic rendering is intentionally retained, build a separately fixture-tested compatibility search rather than silently mixing field contracts.
- **Rule ID or name is null:** inspect raw XML and installed add-on knowledge on parsing/search tiers. Confirm event boundaries and `renderXml=true`; do not substitute display text parsed from a localized Message field when stable XML fields are available.
- **No actor or port appears:** expected. These event schemas do not contain those fields. Correlate other telemetry and current firewall state instead of filling them with `UNKNOWN` and implying the value was logged.
- **GPO rule changes are missing:** expected for per-rule 4946–4948 according to Microsoft. Monitor policy application and effective-state drift through a separately designed control.
- **Operational event IDs differ by Windows build:** keep them outside this primary audit contract. Microsoft documentation for 4946–4948 is the stable basis here; do not remap 2033 to “firewall disabled.”
- **Duplicate results:** compare originating computer, EventRecordID, `_raw`, and `_indextime`; investigate local plus WEF collection, checkpoint reset, replay, or duplicate forwarding. Repair collection before adding `dedup`.
- **Current rule cannot be found:** deletion is expected after 4948, and names/IDs can change during delete/recreate workflows. Use pre-change inventory, the raw event, and change records; do not conclude the event is false.
- **A result says `modified` but settings are unknown:** 4947 proves the documented rule-modification event, not which property changed. Obtain before/after inventory or management-system records.
- **Alert volume is high during deployments:** preserve base reporting, measure exact rule IDs/actions/endpoints, and add bounded downstream exceptions tied to deployment jobs. Never suppress all events from an installer account because actor is not present in this payload.
grandmaExplanation: We record when a Windows computer says one of its local firewall rules was added, changed, or removed. That helps the team check the rule against approved work, while remembering that this diary entry does not say who made the change or show every setting in the rule.
hardware: In-scope Microsoft Windows client and server endpoints running Windows Defender Firewall and producing Security audit events 4946–4948. Domain controllers may be included as endpoints, but network appliances, third-party host firewalls, and cloud-native firewall control planes require separate use cases.
